teams.name: Baltimore Black Sox
teams.fate: Folded; a different team used the Black Sox name in 1934.
teams.note: Wikipedia says this club played 1933-34; league lists treat 1934 as a separate Black Sox II.

teams.name: Columbus Blue Birds
teams.fate: Disbanded mid-season and merged with the Akron Grays.

teams.name: Akron Black Tyrites
teams.fate: Became the Cleveland Giants later in 1933.
teams.note: Name used briefly mid-season by the merged Akron Grays and Columbus club.

teams.name: Cleveland Giants
teams.fate: Finished Columbus's 1933 schedule, then folded.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Moved to Detroit in April 1933 as the Detroit Stars.
teams.note: League lists show this club only briefly in 1933 before the move.

teams.name: Detroit Stars
teams.fate: Dropped from the league after 1933.
teams.note: Formerly the Indianapolis ABCs; its Detroit-area home is recorded as Hamtramck.

teams.name: Cole's American Giants
teams.fate: Left the league; played independently in 1936, then joined the Negro American League.

teams.name: Nashville Elite Giants
teams.fate: Moved to Columbus, Ohio, for 1935.

teams.name: Columbus Elite Giants
teams.fate: Moved to Washington, D.C., for 1936.

teams.name: Washington Elite Giants
teams.fate: Moved to Baltimore for 1938.

teams.name: Baltimore Elite Giants
teams.fate: Joined the Negro American League for 1949.
teams.note: Wikipedia also lists Oriole Park as a secondary home in 1938-44.

teams.name: Pittsburgh Crawfords
teams.fate: Moved to Toledo in the Negro American League for 1939.
teams.note: Charter league members owned by Gus Greenlee, who built Greenlee Field.

teams.name: Homestead Grays
teams.fate: Principal base shifted to Washington, D.C., from 1943.
teams.note: Also used Greenlee Field 1935-37 and Griffith Stadium from 1940; 1933 membership ended early and 1934 was independent.

teams.name: Homestead Grays
teams.fate: Played as an independent after the league folded in 1948.
teams.note: Majority of home games in Washington; Forbes Field still used for Pittsburgh dates.

teams.name: Philadelphia Bacharach Giants
teams.fate: Left the league and returned to independent play in 1935.

teams.name: Philadelphia Stars
teams.fate: Joined the Negro American League for 1949.
teams.note: Played some games at Shibe Park; after 1947 used area parks such as Wilmington Park.

teams.name: Cleveland Red Sox
teams.fate: Dropped from the league after 1934.

teams.name: Baltimore Black Sox
teams.fate: Folded after one season in the league.
teams.note: A separate club using the Black Sox name after the original team disbanded.

teams.name: Newark Dodgers
teams.fate: Merged with the Brooklyn Eagles to form the Newark Eagles.
teams.note: Wikipedia's Newark Eagles page names other parks (Bloomfield, Irvington); the Newark parks list gives Meadowbrook Oval.

teams.name: Brooklyn Eagles
teams.fate: Merged with the Newark Dodgers to form the Newark Eagles.

teams.name: Newark Eagles
teams.fate: Joined the Negro American League and moved to Houston for 1949.
teams.note: Owned by Abe and Effa Manley.

teams.name: New York Cubans
teams.fate: Dropped from the league after 1936; returned in 1939.
teams.note: Also played some home games at Dyckman Oval in Manhattan.

teams.name: New York Cubans
teams.fate: Joined the Negro American League for 1949.
teams.note: Also used Yankee Stadium in 1941-46; won the 1947 Negro World Series.

teams.name: New York Black Yankees
teams.fate: Disbanded after the 1948 season.
teams.note: 1936 and 1939 homes uncertain; the club played mostly in Rochester in 1948. Also used the Polo Grounds.

teams.name: Washington Black Senators
teams.fate: Not in the league after 1938.
teams.note: Formed to fill the gap left when the Elite Giants moved to Baltimore.

teams.name: Harrisburg-St. Louis Stars
teams.fate: Left the league in July to barnstorm; disbanded after 1943.
teams.note: Played as the Bond Bombers for war bond fundraising after leaving the league.

teams.name: Birmingham Black Barons
teams.fate: Did not play in the league in 1939.

teams.name: Birmingham Black Barons
teams.fate: Remained in the league into the 1950s.
teams.note: Rejoined the league in 1940.

teams.name: Chicago American Giants
teams.fate: Remained in the league into the 1950s.
teams.note: Left South Side Park after a December 1940 fire.

teams.name: Cincinnati Tigers
teams.fate: Folded after the 1937 season.

teams.name: Detroit Stars
teams.fate: Quit the league after one season.

teams.name: Indianapolis Athletics
teams.fate: Renamed Indianapolis ABCs for 1938.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Moved to St. Louis as the Stars for 1939.
teams.note: Finances forced a quick move.

teams.name: Atlanta Black Crackers
teams.fate: Moved to Indianapolis for 1939 as the ABCs.
teams.note: Won the second-half title; sometimes used college fields on Crackers game days.

teams.name: Indianapolis ABCs
teams.fate: Disbanded after the 1939 season.
teams.note: The fourth team to use the ABCs name; formerly the Atlanta Black Crackers.

teams.name: Kansas City Monarchs
teams.fate: Remained in the league into the 1960s.
teams.note: Charter league member; the park was named Ruppert Stadium then Blues Stadium.

teams.name: Memphis Red Sox
teams.fate: Remained in the league into the 1960s.
teams.note: Wikipedia infobox lists Russwood Park as home in 1945-47; Martin Stadium used throughout here.

teams.name: St. Louis Stars
teams.fate: Folded after the 1937 season.
teams.note: Finished 5-32 in the league's first year.

teams.name: St. Louis Stars
teams.fate: Renamed St. Louis-New Orleans Stars for 1940.
teams.note: The former Indianapolis ABCs moved to St. Louis.

teams.name: St. Louis-New Orleans Stars
teams.fate: Did not play in 1942; players dispersed to other clubs.
teams.note: Split home games with New Orleans (Pelican Stadium).

teams.name: Jacksonville Red Caps
teams.fate: Moved to Cleveland as the Bears for 1939.

teams.name: Cleveland Bears
teams.fate: Returned to Jacksonville as the Red Caps for 1941.

teams.name: Jacksonville Red Caps
teams.fate: Dropped out of the league in July 1942.

teams.name: Toledo Crawfords
teams.fate: Renamed Toledo-Indianapolis Crawfords for 1940.
teams.note: Former Pittsburgh Crawfords franchise.

teams.name: Toledo-Indianapolis Crawfords
teams.fate: Folded after the 1940 season.
teams.note: Opened in Toledo at Swayne Field, then moved to Indianapolis mid-season.

teams.name: Cincinnati-Cleveland Buckeyes
teams.fate: Moved to Cleveland and renamed Cleveland Buckeyes for 1943.
teams.note: Wikipedia's infobox also lists League Park for 1942; text gives Crosley Field.

teams.name: Cleveland Buckeyes
teams.fate: Moved to Louisville for 1949.
teams.note: Won the 1945 Negro World Series.

teams.name: Cincinnati Clowns
teams.fate: Renamed Cincinnati-Indianapolis Clowns for 1944.

teams.name: Cincinnati-Indianapolis Clowns
teams.fate: Moved fully to Indianapolis and renamed Indianapolis Clowns for 1946.
teams.note: Split home games between Cincinnati and Indianapolis.

teams.name: Indianapolis Clowns
teams.fate: Remained in the league through 1954 and kept barnstorming afterward.
teams.note: Wikipedia's infobox lists Crosley Field through 1947 and Victory Field from 1944.

parks.name: Griffith Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1965; Howard University Hospital now occupies the site.
notable: Home of the Homestead Grays from 1940, plus the Washington Elite Giants and Black Senators.
Rebuilt in steel and concrete within months after a 1911 fire destroyed the wooden park.

parks.name: Forbes Field
parks.status: Demolished in 1971; University of Pittsburgh buildings stand on the site, with part of the outfield wall surviving.
notable: Pittsburgh Pirates home that the Homestead Grays also used for home games.
Opened as one of the first concrete-and-steel ballparks, built in about four months.

parks.name: Greenlee Field
parks.status: Demolished after 1938; the Bedford Dwellings housing project now covers the site.
notable: Built and owned by Crawfords owner Gus Greenlee, one of few Black-built major-level ballparks.
Satchel Paige pitched to Josh Gibson at the April 1932 opening.

parks.name: Ruppert Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1967; a food products plant now occupies the site.
notable: Home of the Newark Eagles from 1936 to 1948, shared with the Newark Bears of the International League.
Opened as Davids' Stadium, later Bears Stadium, before taking the Ruppert name in 1932.

parks.name: Bugle Field
parks.status: Dismantled in 1949; Rockland Industries now has its headquarters and plant on the site.
notable: Primary home of the Baltimore Elite Giants from 1938; the Black Sox also played here.
Owned by the Washington Senators' owners; Joe Cambria renovated it and added lights in 1932.

parks.name: Rickwood Field
parks.status: Still standing as a preserved working ballpark and museum that hosts an annual game.
notable: Oldest surviving professional ballpark in the United States.
Shared by the Birmingham Black Barons and the white Birmingham Barons.

parks.name: Martin Stadium
parks.status: Sold in 1960 and demolished in 1961; a truck dealer occupies the site, which has a historical marker.
notable: Built in 1923 by Red Sox owner Robert S. Lewis as Lewis Park.
Renamed Martin Stadium after the Martin brothers bought the team in 1927; expanded in 1947.

parks.name: Comiskey Park
parks.status: Demolished in 1991; a parking lot for Rate Field marks the site with a home plate marker.
notable: Most frequent host of the Negro leagues' East-West All-Star Game from 1933 to 1960.
The Chicago American Giants made it their home from 1941.

parks.name: South Side Park
parks.status: Damaged by fire in 1940; the Wentworth Gardens housing project now stands on the site.
notable: Hosted games of the 1906 World Series between the White Sox and Cubs.
Home of the Chicago American Giants through 1940, when fire ended its use.

parks.name: Municipal Stadium (Kansas City)
parks.status: Demolished in 1976; a garden and housing redevelopment now occupy the site, marked by a plaque.
notable: Opened as Muehlebach Field, then Ruppert Stadium (1937-43) and Blues Stadium (1943-54) before taking the Municipal name.
Home of the Kansas City Monarchs and later the Athletics and Royals.

parks.name: Yankee Stadium (1923)
parks.status: Demolished 2009-2010; Heritage Field, a public park, now occupies the site.
notable: Primary home of the New York Black Yankees from 1940 through 1947.
Also hosted New York Cubans games in the 1940s.

parks.name: Polo Grounds
parks.status: Demolished in 1964; the Polo Grounds Towers public housing complex now stands there.
notable: Main home of the New York Cubans from 1939.
Its horseshoe shape gave very short foul lines and a deep center field.

parks.name: Ebbets Field
parks.status: Demolished starting 1960; the Ebbets Field Apartments opened on the site in 1962.
notable: Home of the 1935 Brooklyn Eagles of the Negro National League.
Hosted the Brooklyn Dodgers until they left for Los Angeles after 1957.

parks.name: Hinchliffe Stadium
parks.status: Reopened in 2023 after renovation; a National Historic Landmark hosting minor-league baseball and soccer.
notable: Main home of the New York Cubans in 1935-36 and the Black Yankees in 1937-38.
Designated a National Historic Landmark in 2013.

parks.name: Crosley Field
parks.status: Demolished starting 1972; commercial buildings and a street now cover the site.
notable: Hosted the Cincinnati Tigers (1937), Buckeyes (1942) and Clowns (1943-45) of the Negro American League.
In 1935 it became the first major-league park to host night games.

parks.name: League Park
parks.status: Restored as a community park with the 1910 ticket house serving as a baseball museum.
notable: Home of the Cleveland Buckeyes from 1942 to 1950 and the 1934 Cleveland Red Sox.
The Buckeyes won the 1945 Negro World Series.

parks.name: Swayne Field
parks.status: Demolished after 1955; the Swayne Field Shopping Center now stands there.
notable: Home of the 1939 Toledo Crawfords and the start of the 1940 Crawfords season.
Named for Noah H. Swayne Jr., who donated the land.

parks.name: Bush Stadium
parks.status: Converted into the Stadium Lofts apartments in 2013; the facade and light towers remain.
notable: Hosted the Indianapolis ABCs, Athletics, Crawfords and, from 1944, the Clowns.
Ivy on its outfield walls inspired the ivy at Wrigley Field.

parks.name: Ponce de Leon Park
parks.status: Demolished in 1966; the Midtown Place strip mall stands on the site.
notable: Home of the 1938 Atlanta Black Crackers, shared with the white Atlanta Crackers.
A magnolia tree in center field stayed in play until 1947.

parks.name: Durkee Field
parks.status: Still in use; National Register-listed and holding a small museum.
notable: Opened as Barrs Field and rebuilt in 1936-37 after a fire.
Home of the Jacksonville Red Caps in 1938 and 1941-42.

parks.name: Hardware Field
parks.status: Site at East 79th Street and Kinsman Road is now housing.
notable: Home of the Cleveland Bears in 1939 and 1940.
Opening year not found; value shown is the first known Negro-league use (1931).

parks.name: Red Bird Stadium
parks.status: Later Cooper Stadium; closed in 2008 and left half-demolished and abandoned by 2021.
notable: Home of the 1933 Columbus Blue Birds and the 1935 Columbus Elite Giants.
Built from the same blueprints as Red Wing Stadium in Rochester.

parks.name: Tom Wilson Park
parks.status: Demolished; the source does not say what occupies the site now.
notable: Built by owner Thomas T. Wilson for the Nashville Elite Giants.
Stood in Trimble Bottom, then Nashville's largest Black community.

parks.name: Red Wing Stadium
parks.status: Demolished in 1997-98; an industrial and office park now occupies the site.
notable: Site of the New York Black Yankees' final 1948 season.
Renamed Silver Stadium in 1968.

parks.name: Passon Field
parks.status: Site at 48th and Spruce Streets is now a West Philadelphia High School football field.
notable: Home of the Philadelphia Bacharach Giants about 1932-34 and the Stars in 1934-35.
Opening year not found; value shown is the first known Negro-league use.

parks.name: 44th and Parkside Ballpark
parks.status: Now Philadelphia Stars Negro League Memorial Park, with a statue, marker and mural.
notable: Home of the Philadelphia Stars from 1936; the Stars lost the lease after 1947 by one account.
Hosted Game 4 of the 1945 Negro World Series.

parks.name: Meadowbrook Oval
parks.status: Site on South Orange Avenue is now West Side High School.
notable: Listed as the home of the Newark Dodgers in 1934-35.
Opening year not found; value shown is first known Negro-league use. Other sources name Sprague or Ollemar fields.

parks.name: Hamtramck Stadium
parks.status: Current condition not verified; located near Dan Street in Hamtramck.
notable: Home of the Detroit Stars in 1930-31 and listed for the 1933 Stars.
The 1933 Stars were the Indianapolis ABCs moved to Detroit in April.

parks.name: Dequindre Park
parks.status: Site on Dequindre Avenue south of Six Mile Road; current use not verified.
notable: Listed as the home site of the 1937 Detroit Stars.
Park name not confirmed; only its location on Dequindre Avenue is recorded.

parks.name: Metropolitan Park
parks.status: Site near North Broadway and Clarence Avenue is now an industrial area.
notable: Formerly Giants Park II; home of the St. Louis Giants in 1920-21.
Home of the 1937 St. Louis Stars of the Negro American League.

parks.name: South End Park
parks.status: Location and current use not found.
notable: Home of the St. Louis Stars in 1939 and the St. Louis half of 1941.
Opening year not found; value shown is first known use.

parks.name: Island Park
parks.status: Located on City Island in the Susquehanna River; current use not verified.
notable: Home of the 1943 Harrisburg-St. Louis Stars of the Negro National League.
Opening year not found; value shown is first known Negro-league use.

parks.name: Luna Park (Luna Bowl)
parks.status: Site near East 110th Street and Woodland Avenue is now housing.
notable: Home of the 1933 Cleveland Giants of the Negro National League.
Opening year not found; value shown is the season of Negro-league use.

parks.name: Freeport Municipal Stadium
parks.status: Current status not verified.
notable: Listed as a 1936 home of the New York Black Yankees.
Details not found; opening year shown is the season of Negro-league use.

parks.name: Home grounds not recorded
parks.status: Home grounds of the Akron club in 1933 are not recorded.
notable: The 1933 Akron club used the Black Tyrites name briefly mid-season.
Opening year shown is only the season of use.
